Higher-order centrality: ranking actions a first-order network cannot rank

honets

2026-08-25

The analytic question

Which actions are central to human–AI pair-programming sessions? The usual instrument is a centrality measure on the transition network: build the network of what-follows-what, run PageRank, read off the ranking.

That instrument fails on these data, and it fails in an instructive way. This tutorial shows why, and what a higher-order network recovers. hon_centrality() computes centralities on the higher-order topology — where a node is not a state but a state together with the memory of how it was reached — and projects them back onto the states, following Scholtes, Wider & Garas (2016). The implementation follows pathpy 2.2.0, that paper’s reference implementation, generalized to the variable-order networks build_hon() produces.

The data are human_long, bundled with honets: 10,796 coded human turns from 429 sessions, nine action codes.

library(honets)
library(cograph)

The first-order network has nothing to say

fo <- build_hon(human_long, action = "code", actor = "session_id",
                time = "timestamp", max_order = 1, min_freq = 5)
fo
## Higher-Order Network (HON)
##   Nodes:        9 (9 first-order states)
##   Edges:        81
##   Max order:    1 (requested 1)
##   Min freq:     5
##   Trajectories: 425
hon_centrality(fo)
##       state  pagerank betweenness closeness
## 1   Command 0.1111111           0         8
## 2   Correct 0.1111111           0         8
## 3 Frustrate 0.1111111           0         8
## 4   Inquire 0.1111111           0         8
## 5 Interrupt 0.1111111           0         8
## 6    Refine 0.1111111           0         8
## 7   Request 0.1111111           0         8
## 8   Specify 0.1111111           0         8
## 9    Verify 0.1111111           0         8

Every measure returns the same value for all nine actions: PageRank exactly 1/9, closeness exactly 8, betweenness exactly 0. This is not a numerical accident. With 10,796 turns spread over nine codes, every one of the 81 possible transitions occurs at least five times, so the first-order network is the complete digraph on nine nodes. Every node has in-degree nine, which forces PageRank to be uniform; every pair of states is one step apart, which forces closeness to be uniform and betweenness to be zero, because a one-step path has no intermediate node.

The conclusion is decisive and negative: on data this dense, the first-order network is structurally incapable of ranking the actions. No choice of centrality measure repairs it — the information is not in the topology.

The higher-order network ranks them

hon <- build_hon(human_long, action = "code", actor = "session_id",
                 time = "timestamp", max_order = 3, min_freq = 5)
hon
## Higher-Order Network (HON)
##   Nodes:        233 (9 first-order states)
##   Edges:        819
##   Max order:    3 (requested 3)
##   Min freq:     5
##   Trajectories: 425
hon_centrality(hon, type = "pagerank")
##       state   pagerank
## 1   Command 0.18365067
## 2   Correct 0.07833723
## 3 Frustrate 0.10421334
## 4   Inquire 0.10991607
## 5 Interrupt 0.06438203
## 6    Refine 0.08850329
## 7   Request 0.09503177
## 8   Specify 0.23396968
## 9    Verify 0.04199591

The same nine actions, now ranked over a 5.6-fold range: Specify holds 23.4% of the flow, Command 18.4%, down to Verify at 4.2%. The topology that produced this has 233 nodes rather than 9 — the extra 224 are memory contexts such as Specify -> Command, each carrying its own distinct continuation distribution.

The ranking exists because the contexts differ, even though the states do not. Where the first-order network sees nine interchangeable hubs, the higher-order network sees which of them recur inside the heavily travelled contexts. Specify and Command lead because the flow keeps returning to them along many distinct memory paths; Verify is visited rarely and from few contexts.

Seeing the ranking

Two pictures, and the choice between them is the whole point of this vignette.

First the network that cannot rank. fo is the complete digraph on nine states — every pair one step apart, every node the same degree. The figure shows why no centrality measure can separate these actions: there is no structure to separate them by.

splot(fo, minimum = 0.05, title = "First-order: saturated, unrankable")

Then the ranking itself. Note what is not plotted here: the higher-order network has 233 nodes and drawing it is an unreadable hairball. hon_centrality() already projects onto the nine states, so the figure is of its tidy return — nine rows, one per action.

pr <- hon_centrality(hon, type = "pagerank", sort_by = "pagerank")
pr$state <- factor(pr$state, levels = rev(pr$state))
ggplot2::ggplot(pr, ggplot2::aes(x = pagerank, y = state)) +
  ggplot2::geom_segment(ggplot2::aes(x = 0, xend = pagerank,
                                     yend = state),
                        colour = "#999999", linewidth = 0.5) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 3.2, colour = "#0072B2") +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 1 / nrow(pr), linetype = "dashed",
                      colour = "#D55E00") +
  ggplot2::annotate("text", x = 1 / nrow(pr), y = 0.7, hjust = -0.1,
                    label = "first-order: all nine sit here",
                    colour = "#D55E00", size = 3.4) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "PageRank (projected to states)", y = NULL,
                title = "Higher-order topology ranks what first-order cannot") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

The dashed line is 1/9 — where the first-order network puts every action. The higher-order reading spreads them over a 5.6-fold range.

Where the ranking comes from

Setting project = FALSE reports the centralities of the higher-order nodes themselves — that is, of the contexts rather than the states.

hon_centrality(hon, type = "pagerank", project = FALSE,
               sort_by = "pagerank", top = 8)
##                            node order   pagerank
## 1            Specify -> Command     2 0.03480103
## 2            Specify -> Specify     2 0.02101455
## 3            Command -> Command     2 0.02085538
## 4            Command -> Specify     2 0.01991084
## 5             Refine -> Specify     2 0.01536272
## 6 Inquire -> Command -> Command     3 0.01244368
## 7            Inquire -> Command     2 0.01232826
## 8            Request -> Inquire     2 0.01182165

The single most central object in these sessions is not an action but a context: Specify -> Command, holding 3.5% of the flow on its own — more than three times any individual first-order node. Below it sit Specify -> Specify and Command -> Command, the two self-repetition contexts, and a third-order context, Inquire -> Command -> Command, already appears in the top eight. Specification followed by commanding is the load-bearing pattern of this corpus, and it is invisible to any first-order summary, which can only report that Specify and Command are both frequent.

Does the projection choice drive the ranking?

A higher-order node spans several states, so its PageRank has to be distributed among them. The default, "scaled", splits it equally (preserving total mass); "last" assigns it entirely to the state actually occupied.

scaled <- hon_centrality(hon, type = "pagerank", projection = "scaled")
last <- hon_centrality(hon, type = "pagerank", projection = "last")
data.frame(state = scaled$state, scaled = scaled$pagerank,
           last = last$pagerank)
##       state     scaled       last
## 1   Command 0.18365067 0.18375557
## 2   Correct 0.07833723 0.07896900
## 3 Frustrate 0.10421334 0.09997477
## 4   Inquire 0.10991607 0.10706961
## 5 Interrupt 0.06438203 0.06198670
## 6    Refine 0.08850329 0.09076024
## 7   Request 0.09503177 0.09258325
## 8   Specify 0.23396968 0.24412812
## 9    Verify 0.04199591 0.04077275

The two agree to within about one percentage point on every action, and the ordering is identical. The ranking is therefore a property of the higher-order topology, not of the projection rule, and can be reported without a projection caveat.

Betweenness and closeness need a sparser network

Both measures were degenerate on the first-order network. They stay degenerate on the full higher-order network, and for the same reason:

hon_centrality(hon, type = c("betweenness", "closeness"))
##       state betweenness closeness
## 1   Command           0         8
## 2   Correct           0         8
## 3 Frustrate           0         8
## 4   Inquire           0         8
## 5 Interrupt           0         8
## 6    Refine           0         8
## 7   Request           0         8
## 8   Specify           0         8
## 9    Verify           0         8

The projection maps every ordered pair of states to a one-step path, because a second-order node exists for essentially every pair. With no intermediate nodes on any shortest path, betweenness is zero everywhere and closeness is a constant 8. Unlike PageRank, these two measures depend only on the reachability structure, and reachability here is saturated.

Raising min_freq keeps only the well-evidenced transitions, which restores a topology with genuine distances:

sparse <- build_hon(human_long, action = "code", actor = "session_id",
                    time = "timestamp", max_order = 3, min_freq = 80)
sparse
## Higher-Order Network (HON)
##   Nodes:        17 (9 first-order states)
##   Edges:        49
##   Max order:    3 (requested 3)
##   Min freq:     80
##   Trajectories: 425
hon_centrality(sparse, type = c("betweenness", "closeness"))
##       state betweenness closeness
## 1   Command  12.4166667  7.000000
## 2   Correct   1.2500000  6.000000
## 3 Frustrate   1.5833333  6.000000
## 4   Inquire   0.6666667  5.500000
## 5 Interrupt   0.0000000  4.333333
## 6    Refine   0.0000000  5.333333
## 7   Request   0.8333333  6.500000
## 8   Specify  22.2500000  7.500000
## 9    Verify   0.0000000  5.000000

On the 17-node network of transitions seen at least 80 times, the measures separate sharply. Specify brokers 22.3 shortest paths and Command 12.4, while Interrupt, Refine and Verify broker none at all: the well-evidenced routes between actions run through the two directive codes, and the remaining actions sit at the ends of those routes rather than along them. Closeness ranks the same two highest (7.5 and 7.0), confirming that they are also the easiest actions to reach.

Note what this costs: the sparse network describes only the strongest transitions, so it answers a narrower question than the PageRank analysis above. Report the threshold with the result.

When to use which

  • hon_centrality(hon) — the question is which states carry flow, and the sequences have memory. PageRank is the measure to trust on dense data; betweenness and closeness require a topology with real distances, so check for saturation (all-zero betweenness, constant closeness) before interpreting them.
  • project = FALSE — the question is which contexts dominate. Often the more useful table, and the only place where a pattern like Specify -> Command can appear at all.
  • build_hon(max_order = 1) — the first-order baseline. Always run it: the gap between it and the higher-order ranking is the evidence that memory matters, and if there is no gap, the simpler model should be reported.
  • bootstrap_hon() — before reporting a higher-order ranking, check that the rules producing it survive resampling.
  • markov_order_test() — the prior question of whether memory exists at all, as a single global test.

References

  • Scholtes, I., Wider, N., & Garas, A. (2016). Higher-order aggregate networks in the analysis of temporal networks: path structures and centralities. The European Physical Journal B, 89, 61.
  • Xu, J., Wickramarathne, T. L., & Chawla, N. V. (2016). Representing higher-order dependencies in networks. Science Advances, 2(5), e1600028.
  • Scholtes, I. (2017). When is a network a network? Multi-order graphical model selection in pathways and temporal networks. KDD 2017.
